title: kb entry — one atomic claim (4.3)
description: One claim per file. The store is authoritative for knowledge (P14) whether or not a librarian agent exists to serve it.

kind.description: A dimensionless_group and a derived_quantity both carry a formula instead of a value (5.7); what separates them is a claim, not a filing convenience. dimensionless_group asserts the formula evaluates to a pure number. derived_quantity is a named quantity computed from others that KEEPS a dimension, and it states that dimension in `unit`. Until derived_quantity existed there was no kind for the second, so it was filed as the first -- tau_d, whose formula is a length squared over a diffusivity and therefore a TIME, sat under dimensionless_group with no unit anywhere on it.

symbol.description: dimensionless_group and derived_quantity. One symbol means one definition across the store and every card (check 36), whatever its dimension.

unit.description: derived_quantity only: the unit the formula yields, from contracts/units.json. A dimensionless_group must not carry one -- being dimensionless is the claim it makes, and a unit beside it would contradict the kind rather than annotate it.

inputs.description: What the entry was computed from -- and it means two different things depending on the kind, which is the seam check 62 found on 2026-09-20. On a `derived_quantity` or a `dimensionless_group` these are the FORMAL PARAMETERS of the formula: free variables, not references to anything in the store, and no grade composes from them (`tau_d` is E4 in a store holding no diameter). On a `claim` they are QUANTITIES the inference rests on, named so their grades compose to max(E4, worst). Binding the first kind to whatever entry happens to carry the same string is task 020's refused option 2 arriving through a side door: rename one variable in a formula and a grade appears. A claim resting on other CLAIMS uses `supports` instead, because a claim carries no number to compose.

supports.description: What an inference rests on when what it rests on is not a quantity. Added 2026-09-20 at the librarian seat's request, after `declared_versus_inferred_temperature` had its three supports recorded in `validity_conditions` as prose -- the same shape as the CV that computed as 200 per cent, and the reason a distinction living only in prose is one nothing can act on. `inputs` could not hold them: check 62 builds its carriers from `numbers[].name`, two of those supports carry no numbers at all, and the third is a premise about the simulation engine that this store does not hold and should not. Writing them as inputs would have produced three carried-by-nothing rows for things that are not quantities and never will be. Mutually exclusive with `inputs`: arithmetic over quantities and support by claim are different relations and an entry does exactly one of them.

entry.description: an entry_id in this store. Its own grade is what caps the inference.

external.description: a premise this store does not hold and has no business holding -- another agent's, or the person's. One of these stops the grade composing, because an ungraded premise cannot cap anything, and that is the honest report rather than a number that quietly ignores it.

who_could_confirm.description: required beside `external`: a premise outside the store that names nobody who could settle it is not a support, it is a hope. Usually an agent name.

validity_conditions.description: under what conditions the claim holds; a claim without them is not reusable

validity.description: the machine-readable half of validity_conditions (4.3.1). Where the two disagree this one wins (P3): prose cannot be matched against a query condition_range. An entry without it comes back as `overlap: no_overlap` rather than matching silently.

source.description: Where the claim came from, in the same form a card's number uses (5.3), so that an entry's grade is DERIVED and not self-reported (check 43). source_ref says which document; this says what kind of evidence it is, and only the second one fixes a grade. Optional while the store catches up: entries written before the field existed are counted rather than failed.

grade_tag.description: the sub-rank inside a grade, mostly to separate the kinds of E3 (4.3). Its load-bearing use is the citation order among literature: peer_reviewed -> textbook -> vendor_spec -> preprint. The other values exist so the enum is not silently incomplete -- an operator reading is E3 by 5.3 and had no value here, so every such entry left this null and a null read as an omission rather than a kind. Two E5 values added 2026-09-19, for the reason this enum exists at all: `assumed:` sources had no tag, so every one left this null and a null read as an omission rather than a kind -- the same hole operator_read had. `person_ruling` is separated from plain `assumed` and from `operator_recall` because what MOVES them differs, which is the criterion 5.3 used to split read from recall. A recall is settled by asking the person again. A placeholder assumption is settled by getting the datum. A ruling -- the person's reasoned judgement from named evidence, like the 2026-09-19 identification of the bottle -- is overturned only by new evidence, and asking again returns the same answer because it was never a memory. All three are E5; the tag says what would change them.

identifiers.description: Exact names for the thing the claim is about: part_number, lot, catalog_number, position, slot. A nominal designation is exact by definition and carries no uncertainty (5.3), so it belongs here and never in numbers[]. Until this existed a table with part numbers could not become an entry at all, which is why the objective and particle registries stayed in staging. Keys here are split by `addressable_identifiers` below: some may be looked up, most may not.

additionalProperties.description: a string even when it looks like a number. A position stored as 0 invites arithmetic on positions and a magnification stored as 20 invites a decimal point; the driver converts at the call site.

kind.description: Which registry `id` is drawn from. device: a channel, element or RETIRED row id in the device table -- retired ids count, because a fact about hardware that was taken out is exactly the fact someone comes looking for later. configuration: an id in the optical path table. observable: an id in contracts/observables.json. quantity: a name used in numbers[] somewhere in the repository, which is the weakest of the four -- it is a de facto registry rather than a declared one, and it is named here so nobody mistakes it for a checked namespace of its own. sample: an id in the sample table, kb/staging/samples.v0.json -- INSTANCES, the bottle on the bench, not products. Added 2026-09-19 after check 44 refused the subject on every bead entry and the seat removed the field rather than gaming it; the claim then reappeared in the entry NAMES, where nothing checks it. It resolves against that table and nothing else -- deliberately not the way `quantity` resolves, which accepts a name used in numbers[] anywhere and so lets an entry be its own registry. That failed the same day: renaming a number dangled five subjects that had only ever resolved against a number in the same file.

subject.description: What this entry is ABOUT, so a query can find it without already knowing its id. Each subject names its registry rather than being a bare string: two entries calling one thing by different words would make matching a coincidence, and a free list is a string nothing checks. The information is mostly written already as a naming habit -- `csuw1_port_slots` contains `csuw1_port` -- and that habit works until somebody names one differently. Without this field an entry answers only to its own id, its symbol and the names in numbers[]: on 2026-09-18 that left 14 of 25 entries, every one a device fact, reachable only by an id the caller had to learn by reading the staging table first. Optional until the store has filled it; the value arrives with the check that every subject resolves, not with the field.

valid_until.description: When this claim stops being asserted. Required for a `calibration:` source and optional otherwise. §5.3 lists E2 as `calibration:<cal_id>` with a validity period and a condition range BOTH required, and until 2026-09-19 neither was enforced -- so a calibration could claim the second-highest grade in the scale with nothing holding the claim up. It lands before its first subject: no entry carries a calibration source yet, so nothing has to migrate. `date` and `event` both exist because a real calibration ends one of two ways, and refusing the second would refuse correct work: an expiry the operator set, or the next calibration superseding it. One of the two is enough; neither is not.

date.description: the day after which the claim is not asserted

event.description: the occurrence that ends it, e.g. the next recalibration of this objective. The superseding entry then names this one in `supersedes`.

conflict_with.description: contradictory entries are both kept and marked, never merged (4.3)

refuted_by.description:
Entries that DISPROVE this one. Not `conflict_with`, which says two claims disagree and leaves the caller to decide by conditions -- that is the right shape when both could be true somewhere, and the wrong one when an observation on this bench showed a published value false here. Not `supersedes` either: nothing replaced this entry, it is simply wrong.

Added 2026-09-19 for the vendor's 620/680, which two independent measurements on two instruments contradict. Marked as a conflict, kb_conflicts told the caller to pick -- and picking is exactly what there is no longer a choice about.

**The entry stays and its grade does not move.** Rule 8 keeps it so the next person who finds the data sheet meets a record that it was examined; and the grade derives from the source (check 43), so a vendor specification is E3 whether or not it is refuted. A refuted E3 is still an E3 -- which is the whole reason this field has to exist rather than being expressed as a regrade. What changes is not how good the evidence is, it is whether the claim is true here.

Whatever serves this store must carry it in the projection a caller actually reads, beside grade and claim. 21c5325 fixed conflict_with being computed and left out of kb_query's fourteen fields; a refutation nobody sees is the same defect with higher stakes.

refutes.description: The other side of `refuted_by`, on the entry doing the disproving. Both directions are written so a caller arriving from either end sees it, the way conflict_with is symmetric.

curated_by.description: who put it here. Until M3 that is a person, not the librarian agent.

addressable_identifiers.description: Which `identifiers` keys a caller may look an entry up BY. This is a registry the server reads, not a constraint on entries: any key matching propertyNames may be stored, but only these join the names an entry answers to. It exists because the part number -- the string on the barrel, the title of the vendor sheet, the thing an operator would type -- was the one field in an entry that nothing could find. Verified on 2026-09-18 at 25 entries: kb_query('MRD71670') returned 0 and kb_query('Kinetix 22') returned 0, while kb_query('na') returned six objectives that all named subject device:nosepiece and so could not be told apart by address at all.
addressable_identifiers.criterion: Does reconfiguring the instrument change this value? If yes it is never addressable. A part number survives a lens swap; a slot number is falsified by one, and nothing in the store records that someone turned the nosepiece. An addressable placement would hand back a stale answer at full confidence, which is worse than not finding it. The curator had already written this argument into nosepiece_objective_assignment: position-to-lens is the one claim on that device a single swap falsifies.
addressable_identifiers.closed: The list is closed and the default is not-addressable, so a key invented later does not silently become a query surface. Growing it is a deliberate edit with a reason, the way observables.json and goal.schema.json's purposes grow.
addressable_identifiers.class_handles: Some of these name a class rather than an item -- `model` is Kinetix 22 for both cameras, `product` is a product line, `immersion` is shared by every oil lens. That is not a reason to exclude them: kb_query already returns sets and a caller reads `identifiers` on each row. It is recorded here so a hit's kind is not mistaken for uniqueness.

allOf.$comment: 5.3 lists E2 as `calibration:<cal_id>` with a validity period AND a condition range, both required, and neither was enforced until 2026-09-19. `validity` is the machine-readable half that matching actually reads, so requiring only the prose would leave the range unusable. What separates E2 from E5 is that a calibration event happened and is bounded: an unbounded calibration is a measurement with no event, which is the same claim an operator could have made from memory. AMENDED 2026-09-19: `validity` is required OR the entry names a `sample` subject. 5.3 asks a calibration for a condition range because a claim without conditions gets applied where it does not hold -- the pixel size holds at 1x1 binning and nowhere else. But a calibration whose scope is WHICH OBJECT has no interval: the person measured this bottle's diameter, and the thing that stops it being applied to another bottle is the subject, not a range. The scope lives in `subject` when the scope is an object. `valid_until` stays required unconditionally, because that is what carries the event -- an unbounded calibration is a measurement with no event, which was always the load-bearing half.

inputs and supports are mutually exclusive. Composing arithmetic over quantities and resting on claims are different relations; an entry doing both would leave check 62 no way to say which cap applied.
